visual_beats.directive: Show the bar alone on a plain background
Shopper grid fades in and groups separate
Title resolves into four chapter tiles

narration.text: Meet Verdant Crunch, a young plant based snack brand facing one question. Who wants a pea protein bar, and why? Marketing is identifying customer wants and satisfying them profitably. On screen, a crowd of shoppers splits into groups, needs turn into products, and market share gets measured. We will see mass and niche markets, segmentation tiles and how competition changes choices. By the end, you can judge which route gives this small brand the strongest position.

visual_beats.directive: Need icon pulses at the top of the loop
Product node lights and satisfaction halo spreads
Income slider moves and premium line appears

narration.text: Marketing starts with customer needs. Verdant Crunch listens, then satisfies those needs with a tasty, affordable bar. Satisfied buyers repeat purchase, and repeat buying builds customer loyalty. Communicating with customers builds relationships, and relationships keep sales steady. Because household incomes rose, therefore more shoppers wanted premium ingredients, so the firm added a smaller premium line. Marketing also means anticipating changes in customer needs, before rivals spot them. Watch the loop: need, product, satisfaction, loyalty, relationship, then need again.

visual_beats.directive: Axes and ring outline draw in
Numbers slide into the ratio 1.6 over 8
One fifth of the ring fills in gold

narration.text: Market share is the percentage of total market sales or revenue held by one brand. Here the health snack market sells two million packs a year at four dollars each, giving eight million dollars of sales. Verdant Crunch sells four hundred thousand packs, worth one point six million dollars. One point six divided by eight, times one hundred, gives twenty percent. The ring fills to show that share. Share shows competitive strength, not profit. More rivals now enter, so the firm must differentiate or cut its price.

visual_beats.directive: Crowd divides down the middle
Mass cart fills with many bars
Niche cart fills with fewer premium bars

narration.text: Now the audience splits. On the left, a mass market sells to the largest part of the market, often with standardised products. Verdant Crunch could supply every supermarket, winning high volume and economies of scale. On the right, a niche market is a small, specialised segment of a much larger market, say older athletes needing low sugar snacks. There is less competition, but limited volume. Two carts move across the screen: the mass cart holds thousands of bars, the niche cart holds hundreds at a higher price.

visual_beats.directive: Age and income tiles snap in
Location, gender and lifestyle tiles follow
Funnel focuses into two chosen segments

narration.text: Markets can be segmented by age, income, location, gender and lifestyle. Five tiles slide into place. Age separates students from retirees. Income separates budget from premium buyers. Location separates city from rural shoppers. Gender and lifestyle shape flavour and format choices. Market segmentation means knowing that different segments exist, then developing and marketing different products for each. Targeting improves, because messages fit buyers, but research and production costs rise, because every tile needs its own campaign.

visual_beats.directive: Five driver sliders rise and fall
Demand curve bends right then left
Rival box appears and packaging refreshes

narration.text: Spending patterns shift with income, age, technology, fashion and the economic climate. Animated sliders move and the demand curve bends. When incomes dip, shoppers trade down. When a new trend spreads, they trade up. Some markets become more competitive as rivals copy ideas, and prices fall. Businesses respond by differentiating, improving quality or lowering prices. Because a rival launched a cheaper bar, therefore Verdant Crunch refreshed its packaging, so shoppers noticed a clear difference on the shelf.

visual_beats.directive: Funnel focuses from 2m to 400k
Revenue bar grows to $1.6m
Extra 50k buyers lift the bar again

narration.text: Follow the numbers. Two million packs are sold in the whole market. Verdant Crunch aims at gym goers and busy students, and reaches four hundred thousand buyers. At four dollars a pack, revenue is one point six million dollars, which is twenty percent of the eight million dollar market. The funnel focuses from two million shoppers to four hundred thousand buyers. If a niche campaign adds fifty thousand buyers, revenue grows by two hundred thousand dollars. The bar rises, but the campaign costs one hundred thousand dollars.

scenes.title: Mass Reach Or Niche Focus
labels: Mass: volume and scale, but price wars
Niche: focus and loyalty, but small

visual_beats.directive: Two columns of pros and cons appear
Scale tips toward the niche side
Verdict banner slides up

narration.text: Time to weigh both sides. A mass market brings high volume and economies of scale, yet it needs heavy spending and invites price wars. A niche market brings focus and less competition, yet volume stays small and a trend can fade. Segmentation sharpens targeting, but every extra segment adds research and production cost. Because the brand is small, therefore it should start niche, so it can learn before expanding. The verdict is to begin focused, then reach for the mass market once the recipe is proven.

recap_quiz.question: Verdant Crunch sells 400,000 packs at $4 in a 2,000,000-pack market. Total market revenue is $8m. What is its market share?
recap_quiz.visual_explanation: A ring chart fills one fifth of the market while 1.6 million and 8 million slide into the ratio on screen.
